meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The saddest aspect of life right now is that science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Asimov: printed as a chapter epigraph on p. 281 of Isaac Asimov's Book of Science and Nature Quotations (1988), verified with scans.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Asimov wrote it himself. The line is printed as the epigraph opening Chapter 72, “Science and Society,” on page 281 of Isaac Asimov’s Book of Science and Nature Quotations (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1988), which he edited with Jason A. Shulman. Quote Investigator ↗ verified that page with scans and concludes Asimov deserves credit for the remark he published in 1988.

source.excerpt: The saddest aspect of life right now is that science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom.
trail: 1988 — the source. Quote Investigator ↗ cites the line at quote page 281 of Isaac Asimov’s Book of Science and Nature Quotations, Chapter 72: Science and Society, as the chapter epigraph — and marks the citation “Verified with scans.”

The book is real and catalogued. The Internet Archive record ↗ confirms the edition: Isaac Asimov’s Book of Science and Nature Quotations, associated name Jason Shulman, Weidenfeld & Nicolson, New York, 1988.

2006 — the anthologies pick it up. Quote Investigator logs it credited to Asimov in Geoff Tibballs’s The Mammoth Book of Zingers, Quips and One-Liners (p. 562) and Reader’s Digest’s Treasury of Wit & Wisdom (p. 146), both verified with scans ↗.

2011 — the wording drifts. Michio Kaku quoted it in Physics of the Future (p. 350) as “The saddest aspect of society right now…” — expressly prefaced “As Isaac Asimov once said,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The book is an anthology of other people’s science and nature quotations, but this sentence is Asimov’s own: it stands as the epigraph at the head of the “Science and Society” chapter rather than as an entry credited to someone else.

author.name: Isaac Asimov
author.heading: Who was Isaac Asimov?
author.bio: Isaac Asimov was born in Russia around 2 January 1920, naturalised as a U.S. citizen in 1928, and became both a professor of biochemistry and one of the most prolific authors in publishing history — Wikipedia records that he wrote or edited more than 500 books. He is best known for the Foundation series and I, Robot, but the bulk of his output was non-fiction: popular science, history, and reference works aimed squarely at the general reader. He died on 6 April 1992.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The author is right; the wording is what travels badly. Two altered forms circulate widely, and the second one travels inside a Michio Kaku paragraph, which is where the wording drift comes from.

items.who: “Science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom.”
items.why: The headless version, stripped of “The saddest aspect of life right now is that,” circulates on unsourced quote sites — for example this Goodreads entry ↗, which gives no book source at all. The sentiment survives; the printed sentence does not.
Michio Kaku printed this variant on page 350 of Physics of the Future (2011), attributing it to Asimov, as Quote Investigator documents ↗. The 1988 book reads “life,” not “society.”

Because the line reached many readers through Physics of the Future, Kaku is sometimes taken for its author. He is not: the passage ↗ quotes it explicitly — “As Isaac Asimov once said” — inside a longer paragraph that Goodreads bylines to Michio Kaku, which is exactly how the confusion starts.

misattribution.truthLine: Isaac Asimov wrote it, and the accurate wording is the 1988 one: “The saddest aspect of life right now is that science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom” — verified with scans at p. 281 ↗.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: It is an odd little fact that one of the most-quoted lines about the limits of science was published in a book of other people’s quotations. Asimov and Jason A. Shulman assembled the 1988 anthology from centuries of scientists and writers, and, as Quote Investigator records, the book’s 86 sections each open with a quotation from Asimov himself. This one heads the chapter called “Science and Society.”

That placement explains the shape of the sentence. It is not an aphorism polished for a lecture hall; it is an editor’s framing note, written to set up a chapter, and it carries the flat resignation of someone who had spent decades explaining research to the public and watching the public do what it liked with it.
context.detailsSummary: How to cite it without repeating the common errors
detailsBody: Use “life,” not “society,” in the opening clause — the “society” form is a later variant, documented in Michio Kaku’s Physics of the Future (2011).
Cite the book, not a quote site: Isaac Asimov’s Book of Science and Nature Quotations, ed. Isaac Asimov and Jason A. Shulman (New York: Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1988), 281.
Keep the full sentence. The truncated “Science gathers knowledge faster than society gathers wisdom” is a paraphrase of a real line, not the line.
